name: Sayula Popoluca

Salt Lake City: University of Utah Press, p. 81, 'Sayula Popoluca Primary Stress' (an analysis of the forms in Clark 1961); carried in Google Books windows (volume d2BkAAAAMAAJ) and restated in van der Hulst, Harry, Rob Goedemans & Ellen van Zanten (eds.). 2010. A Survey of Word Accentual Patterns in the Languages of the World. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton, Mixe-Zoque paragraph (section number not visible in the excerpt; volumes AZGUEQmFqfMC / emVnZA8KPQwC). catalog_locator: Wichmann 1995: 81 (running header 'Proto-Mixe-Zoquean 81'), section 'STRESS', subsection 'Sayula Popoluca Primary Stress'. The whole passage, from 'Although both SaP and OlP verge toward having phonemic stress' to the opening of the Kaufman quotation, is covered continuously by overlapping Google Books windows (volume d2BkAAAAMAAJ). Rule labels PRECEDE their rules: (Sa/1a) rightmost heavy syllable in the word string; (Sa/1b) or else the leftmost syllable in the rightmost root; (Sa/2) certain inherently accented suffixes override; (Sa/3) Spanish loans take Spanish stress and are not affected by (Sa/1). Between the Kaufman quotation and the secondary-stress passage Wichmann lists and discusses the SaP forms that do not follow these rules, closing 'The list above is not longer than what is to be expected. More important, the exceptions are not arbitrary, as are the (far more numerous) exceptions to Kaufman's rules. They generate specific hypotheses about the history of Sayula Popoluca'. Secondary stress: 'Secondary stress seems to be assigned cyclically.. Since examples are scanty, this rule must be tentative' (the windows read '.. history of Sayula Popoluca. Secondary stress seems..', so whether 'Sayula Popoluca Secondary Stress' stands as the compilation-in heading cannot be read from them), followed by the heading 'Oluta Popoluca Stress'. Restatement: van der Hulst, Harry, Keren Rice & Leo Wetzels. 2010. The languages of Middle America, in van der Hulst, Goedemans & van Zanten (eds.), 249-312, §5.2 'Mixe-Zoque', p. 273. Clark 1995 p. 80; Clark 1961 p. vii note I.3 (p. 9).
catalog_quote: Wichmann 1995: 81 (snippet windows, elided): "STRESS Although both SaP and OIP verge toward having phonemic stress, stress assignment rules in both languages can be shown to directly reflect pM stress rules which were automatic. ... Sayula Popoluca Primary Stress The representation of SaP forms in Clark (1961) admits of an analysis of primary stress assignment. It is implied in Clark's works that stress is phonemic. Kaufman (1963), however, views stress as ... rightmost heavy syllable in the word string if any such syllable is present. (A heavy syllable contains V:, V?, or Vh as its nucleus). (Sa/1b) ... leftmost syllable in the rightmost root. (Sa/2). Certain suffixes may override this pattern: inflectional suffixes -wáy ... (Sa/1). This view is directly opposed to that of Kaufman (1963: 41, 2264): "In Sayula stress is generally on the first syllable of the stem unless a suffix with morphophonemic primary stress occurs in the form ... Secondary stress seems to be assigned cyclically according to the same rules as primary stress, provided that there are at least two syllables between ..." | van der Hulst, Goedemans & van Zanten 2010 (snippets): "... Sayula Popoluca accent goes on the rightmost heavy syllable or else to the leftmost syllable in the rightmost root. Certain suffixes are inherently accented (Wichmann 1995: 81)." ... "According to Wichmann (1995: 81): “although both [Sayula and Oluta Popoluca] ..."

new_statements.quote: El acento se escribe como en español. Las palabras que terminan en vocal o en las consonantes n o s tienen el acento en la penúltima sílaba. Las palabras que terminan en una consonante que no sea n o s tienen el acento en la última sílaba. Se escribe el acento cuando es la excepción de la regla. Por ejemplo, no se escribe el acento en las palabras popolucas ma̱šu [má̱šu] manso, camdʉjc [camdʉ́jc] acahual y ma̱yin [má̱yin] pepegua. Pero se escribe en las palabras ámbanu antiguo, cáduts agrio.
new_statements.translation: The accent is written as in Spanish. Words ending in a vowel or in the consonants n or s have the accent on the penultimate syllable. Words ending in a consonant other than n or s have the accent on the last syllable. The accent is written when a word is an exception to the rule. For example, no accent is written on the Popoluca words ma̱šu [má̱šu] 'tame', camdʉjc [camdʉ́jc] 'fallow field' and ma̱yin [má̱yin] 'pepegua'. But it is written on the words ámbanu 'old', cáduts 'sour'.

I rendered pp. 94-96 at 200 dpi and the accent paragraph at 300 dpi and read the images. Printed p. 79 = 'NOTAS GRAMATICALES / POPOLUCA DE SAYULA / 1. Fonologia' (consonant and vowel charts, s-diaeresis, barred-u, underline = long vowel, saltillo, postvocalic j in the nucleus); printed p. 80 (p. 95) ends section 1 with exactly the passage quoted: 'El acento se escribe como en espanol. Las palabras que terminan en vocal o en las consonantes n o s tienen el acento en la penultima silaba. Las palabras que terminan en una consonante que no sea n o s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress position is a property of each word that the practical orthography records: by a Spanish-style convention it is left unmarked when it falls on the penult of a vowel-/n-/s-final word or on the final syllable of a word ending in another consonant, and marked with an acute otherwise (exceptions include initial/antepenultimate stress, e.g. ámbanu, cáduts, and in the same notes újtsat 'nosotros', míjchat 'ustedes', jé'jat 'ellos'). The passage gives no phonological or morphological rule predicting stress; it only implies that most words are penult- or final-stressed and that exceptions exist.
new_statements.exceptions: ámbanu 'antiguo', cáduts 'agrio' carry a written accent as exceptions to the default; pronoun plurals újtsat, míjchat, jé'jat (p. 80) are likewise written with accent (stress on the stem rather than the -at plural suffix).
new_statements.domain_note: Orthographic word / dictionary citation forms. This is a spelling convention in a vocabulary's grammar notes, written by the primary describer of the language, not an explicit phonological analysis; Clark's 1969 Tlalocan text marks stress on every word (final, penult and antepenult positions all occur, e.g. yawayná?, igikupé·ga, iyáhkahaw), consistent with stress being lexically/morphologically rather than positionally fixed. Clark 1959 (Studies in Linguistics 14) and the grammatical outline in Clark 1961 should contain the phonological statement and would supersede this.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Popoluca of Sayula de Alemán, Veracruz (sayu1241 itself; Clark's fieldwork from the 1950s onward). No dialect split is at issue.

new_statements.quote: [p. vi, Phonological Key, after the consonant and vowel charts:] Vowels Front Central Back / high i ʉ u / mid-low e a o / Stress (´) / Vowel length (_) [p. vii:] I. Notes on orthography: ... 3. Unassimilated Spanish loan words carry the same stress as in Spanish and is not written except as used in Spanish orthography. In such words Popoluca speakers tend to lengthen the stressed vowel. This length is not written.

Quote check: p. 8 = printed vi 'Phonological Key' ends exactly with 'Vowels Front Central Back / high i ʉ u / mid-low e a o / Stress (´) / Vowel length (_)'; p. 9 = printed vii, 'I. Notes on orthography.. 3. Unassimilated Spanish loan words carry the same stress as in Spanish and is not written except as used in Spanish orthography. In such words Popoluca speakers tend to lengthen the stressed vowel. This length is not.' -- both verbatim…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with both records. It agrees with the existing statement from Clark 1995 (Vocabulario, p. 80), read as lexical: there too stress is a per-word property, written when it departs from a Spanish-style default; in 1961 Clark simply writes it on every word. It is also the primary data behind the catalog record (Wichmann 1995: 81, classification weight-hedged): Wichmann says SaP 'verge[s] toward having phonemic stress' and that 'the representation of SaP forms in Clark (1961) admits of an analysis of primary stress assignment' -- Clark 1961 itself offers no such analysis, so it neither confirms nor contradicts Wichmann's rule-based (pM automatic stress) reading; no placement conflict i…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Clark 1961 states no stress-placement rule for native words. Stress (acute accent) is listed in the Phonological Key on a par with the segmental phonemes and vowel length, and it is written on every native polysyllable throughout the texts and the glossary, at varying positions (texts p. 1: iguinʉ́mga, na'waywájat, jayuná'jat, i-išcápcapay; glossary p. 199: ámbanu 'ancient', ámpay 'old' [initial], amáyi 'to teach', acmánac 'to lower', actógoy 'to lose' [penult], acyó'y 'to cause to walk', ajcú't 'to send', aguép 'to have' [final]) -- i.e. the work treats stress as phonemic and records it lexically word by word. The only rule stated concerns unassimilated Spanish loans: they keep Spanish stress (written only as Spanish orthography writes it) and speakers lengthen the stressed vowel of such loans (length not written). The morphological outline (pp. 175-197: morphophonemics, compounds, derivation, inflection) says nothing about stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated. Some words in the texts and glossary carry two (or more) acute marks, unlabelled as primary vs secondary, e.g. yošwátcapéy (p. 2), icóšaténajʉ́'jcawá'n (p. 2), acápatú'c 'sideways', ájchiwáy 'old lady' (p. 199).
new_statements.exceptions: Unassimilated Spanish loan words: Spanish stress retained, not marked except per Spanish orthographic convention; stressed vowel of such loans tends to be lengthened, length unwritten (p. vii, note I.3). Sounds f, v, d, k, ñ, ll, x, h occur only in Spanish loans (p. vii, note I.2).
new_statements.identity_note: Sayula Popoluca of the town of Sayula, Veracruz -- 'spoken only in this one town' (Editor's Note, p. iii); texts tape-recorded in Sayula from named bilingual informants (Catalina López c. 65, Carlos Rofino 35, Panuncio Isidoro 25, Fortino Vidaña 25, Santos Antonio 17; Author's Preface p. iv). No dialect division mentioned.

sources.note: Notas gramaticales §1 Fonología, p. 80 (p. 95): accent is written as in Spanish -- words ending in a vowel or n/s are stressed on the penult, words ending in any other consonant on the final syllable, and the acute is written only on exceptions (e.g. ámbanu 'antiguo', cáduts 'agrio'; unwritten in ma̱šu [má̱šu], camdʉjc [camdʉ́jc], ma̱yin [má̱yin]). An orthographic default-plus-exceptions statement, not a phonological rule.

tone.quote: Examples are given in phonological transcription. I indicate here the phonetic realization of some letters used in the transcription; x:[ʃ], j:[h], ’:[ʔ], y:[j]. Sayula Popoluca has six vowels /a, e, i, o, u, ü/ with their long counterparts /aa, ee, ii, oo, uu, üü/. The /ü/ is a high-mid vowel. The letter ‘0’ in examples indicates zero morpheme.
